name: Yara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining firms, AI companies or political groups, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a haul truck, check the dispatch board on my tablet and show new operators the safe turn by the loading face. I use an AI assistant at home to sort my notes for a technical course, but in the cab I still check the radio and the road myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work gives you the most satisfaction, and what is wearing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted to make a quick call when the route gets messy. The shifts are long and the pay is lower than the responsibility suggests; I have less than a month of expenses put aside, so I keep an eye on every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small improvement to dispatch could save me a few minutes on the handover. I would still read the route note myself, because an old warning can matter more than a tidy screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to try the update and compare it with the way we already work. I would also say that a faster board does not change the fact that our pay barely leaves room for surprise bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck work looks steady in this version, and I already use small AI tools without letting them make the safety call. My thin savings still bother me, but this scenario does not give me a reason to expect a lost shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same rotation and use the dispatch update if the crew finds it useful. I would move the next overtime payment into my emergency account instead of buying the new riding jacket I have been eyeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about my small cushion, not about a machine taking the truck in this mild picture. I would tell my teammate Jo that having a useful job and having enough savings are two separate things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting the new dispatch update, and how would you check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it sent us past a barricade or missed a radio closure, I would stop and check the signed route plan with the control room. I would only keep using the update if it saved time without hiding those warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cover first if overtime fell for a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and electricity would come first, then food for the month. I would pause takeout before touching the small amount I have saved for a training fee.

say: I would test the **dispatch update** against our current route notes.
A faster board does not fix **low pay** or surprise bills.
think: The **truck work** still looks steady in this mild picture.
My small savings cushion remains a **separate worry**.
do: Keep my **current rotation** and compare the dispatch update with radio calls.
Move the next overtime payment into my **emergency account**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about my savings, but secure in this version of the job.
S0.quote: I would also say that a faster board does not change the fact that our pay barely leaves room for surprise bills.
fieldNote: Yara already uses everyday AI but keeps **safety checks** in her own hands.
Her **thin savings** concern her even when the haul-truck role seems secure.
She tests tools against **radio and route records** before relying on them.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and compare dispatch notes with radio calls
Move the next overtime payment into the emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine software taking the first pass at route planning, maintenance notes and shift bookings. The truck still needs an operator for now, but a lead job may have fewer planning hours attached to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we should learn the planning tools while the crew still has time to check their work. I would not promise that nobody loses hours, because the mine can keep the trucks and still cut the people who schedule them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift may be less exposed than an office job, but the dispatch and reporting parts are still part of my lead work. I could lose some responsibility or hours, and with few mines nearby I would want another skill before the roster changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the mine's training sandbox to learn how the planner reaches a route choice, then keep a log of cases where my road knowledge changes it. In the first year I would ask for a paid assignment helping the maintenance team check equipment records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a reduction in lead hours would hit my income, even if the truck driving stays. I would delay a holiday and keep my rent account separate until I knew whether the new planner changed headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you that your lead hours are at risk, and who would you ask first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch whether the next shift rota stops listing a lead operator beside each crew. I would ask my supervisor Tomas for the staffing plan before I assumed that a new screen meant a smaller team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner disagreed with your experience on a route, how would you respond?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the suggested route beside the marked route with a spotter before taking a loaded truck through it. If it missed a soft edge or a one-way closure, I would send the example to the trainer and keep using the safe route.

say: We should learn the **planning tools** while we can check the work.
The mine can keep trucks and still cut **scheduling hours**.
think: Route planning and reports are part of my **lead duties**.
Few nearby mines make a lost shift **hard to replace**.
do: Practice in the planner's **training sandbox** and log route disagreements.
Ask for a **paid maintenance assignment** checking equipment records.
feel: I feel **anxious** because lead hours could reduce my income.
S1.quote: I would not promise that nobody loses hours, because the mine can keep the trucks and still cut the people who schedule them.
fieldNote: Yara identifies **planning and reporting** as the likely early change.
She uses **road knowledge** to test the planner rather than reject it outright.
A paid maintenance assignment could build a **second skill** without risking current wages.

steps.text: Practice the route planner in the mine training sandbox and log errors
Request a paid maintenance assignment checking equipment records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That puts thinking AI in the planning room by 2028, then robots in the pit around 2031. I would have two years to make myself useful somewhere else in the mine before the hands-on work changes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the operators that the thinking work changes first and robots follow about three years later. I would ask the mine for a schedule of training and openings, because a warning without a place to move does not pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose planning hours before the robot arrives, and I cannot build much of a financial buffer from my current pay in two years. I am adaptable, though, and my daily use of the dispatch tablet gives me a start in equipment records or maintenance planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask Tomas to let me spend one paid shift a month with maintenance and learn their physical inspection routine. In 2029, if AGI had taken over planning, I would apply for a hands-on service shift while keeping my haul-truck qualification current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing hours, though there is a three-year gap before robots reach hands-on work. I would stop putting money toward a holiday and use overtime to build even a small course fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no equipment-records post opened in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask about hands-on inspection work at the neighboring mine before paying for a course myself. If there were no openings there either, I would keep my license current and take any paid maintenance shadow shift I could get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your current work would you show the maintenance crew first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them the wear pattern I notice when the haul truck turns near the loading face. Then I would ask a mechanic to show me which parts need a physical check before an AI system can read the service record.

say: Thinking AI arrives first; hands-on robots follow about **three years later**.
A warning needs **training and openings**, not only a speech.
think: Planning hours could go before the **robots arrive**.
Physical service work may remain briefly, but future **vacancies are uncertain**.
do: Spend one paid shift each month with **hands-on maintenance**.
In 2029, seek physical service work while keeping my **operator license**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but I can still build a route into maintenance.
S2.quote: I would ask the mine for a schedule of training and openings, because a warning without a place to move does not pay rent.
fieldNote: Yara connects the **two-year runway** to paid hands-on experience.
Her route knowledge could help with **physical checks** before robots arrive.
She checks **neighboring openings** before paying for training herself.

steps.text: Spend one paid shift each month with the mine maintenance crew
Put overtime into a small equipment-course fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to build a record with maintenance if I start now, and robots are still another three years after thinking AI. I would use that time on actual shifts, not wait until the mine announces a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say operators should learn the maintenance side while they can still earn their normal wages. I would also ask for a clear list of which certificates lead to an internal job, because I do not want to study toward a dead end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five-year warning gives me time to move toward inspection planning, which uses both tablet skills and what I know about the equipment. My savings are thin, so the course has to be paid or tied to a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to shadow maintenance one shift a month now and finish a hands-on safety inspection certificate before 2031. In 2032, the first year after AGI arrives, I would ask about physical inspection shifts, but I would not assume that planning or record jobs remain for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because thinking AI could change the planning work, but I would not be waiting with no experience. I would keep the truck shifts until an internal move was approved in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the maintenance lead before choosing the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the certificate is accepted for inspection planning and whether trainees get paid for shadow hours. I would also ask to see a sample work order so I know what the job looks like on a normal day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the first inspection role went to someone else in 2032, what would you do next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the truck and ask for the next opening rather than quit without a wage. I would keep practicing the records system during maintenance shifts and apply at the neighboring mine if a vacancy appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have mentioned inspection planning, but full AGI could do the thinking work in those records. What would still need your hands, and what is uncertain about that route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person may still need to look for wear, feel a vibration or confirm a repair while robots are not yet doing hands-on work. AGI could still handle the records and planning, and I do not know how many physical inspection shifts the mine would keep or what they would pay.

say: Operators should learn maintenance while **normal wages** continue.
I want certificates tied to a **real internal job** at the mine.
think: Physical inspection uses **equipment knowledge**, but records work may be automated.
The number and pay of those **hands-on vacancies** are unknown.
do: Shadow mechanics and earn a **hands-on inspection certificate**.
In 2032, ask about physical inspection shifts before leaving the **truck wage**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but five years lets me build experience before the change.
S3.quote: A person may still need to look for wear, feel a vibration or confirm a repair while robots are not yet doing hands-on work.
fieldNote: Yara shifts from planning to **physical inspection** after the AGI challenge.
She recognizes **records and scheduling** may be done by AGI.
She cannot assume how many **hands-on roles** will remain or what they pay.

steps.text: Earn a hands-on inspection certificate through paid shadow shifts
Check the number and pay of physical inspection openings in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me enough time to become the person the maintenance crew already calls when a truck makes an odd noise. Thinking AI comes around 2036, but hands-on robots are not expected until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we should use the next few years to learn the systems that track machine wear. I would say a long warning is only useful if we can practice the work and qualify for a paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when thinking AGI arrives, so I still have time to build another trade rather than hope the truck lasts forever. Ten years feels manageable if I keep moving, although my thin savings mean I still cannot take unpaid time off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start monthly hands-on maintenance shifts now, finish the safety inspection certificate and save toward a three-month cushion. In 2037, after thinking AGI arrived, I would ask about paid physical inspection work and keep the truck qualification current until robots were closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change, because my job and income look reasonably safe for the next few years. The thin cushion is still on my mind, so I would build it while the roster remains stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof that your ten-year plan is working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to complete the certificate, get some paid maintenance hours and see whether physical inspection posts actually remain after AGI takes over records. If those jobs disappeared or paid too little, I would ask the neighboring mine about other work before spending more on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2037, if no inspection role were available, what would you do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for physical equipment-service work at the neighboring mine and keep building maintenance experience where I am. I would not leave a paid shift until I had a written offer and enough savings to cover a move.

say: Use the lead time to learn **physical equipment checks**.
Practice and a **paid post** make a long warning useful to the crew.
think: At 37, I can build **hands-on experience** before robots arrive.
AGI may automate records; physical vacancies and pay remain **uncertain**.
do: Complete the hands-on inspection certificate and save for a **three-month cushion**.
In 2037, seek physical service work and keep my **truck qualification**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the distant change, while my near-term income looks safe.
S4.quote: I would not leave a paid shift until I had a written offer and enough savings to cover a move.
fieldNote: Yara treats a decade as **usable preparation time**, not a guarantee.
AGI may remove **record tasks** while robots leave a short physical-work window.
She will move only after a **written offer** and enough savings.

steps.text: Complete the hands-on safety inspection certificate before 2031
Set aside overtime until three months of expenses are covered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is not much time to replace planning hours before the robots arrive later. Paid practice with maintenance and a clear list of internal openings would help me build a second skill while I still have wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I use AI every day for small things, so I am not afraid of every new tool. I still want the person operating the truck to have the authority to stop when the road and the screen disagree.

headlineQuote: I still want the person operating the truck to have the authority to stop when the road and the screen disagree.
portrait: Yara Bauer is **27** and operates haul trucks at a large mine.
She is among the best at the job and earns **lower pay** for a team lead.
She has **less than a month** of expenses saved and few nearby alternatives.
She uses **AI tools daily** but keeps safety decisions with the operator.
She is exploring a **hands-on maintenance path**, while recognizing AGI may take records work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut planning hours before Yara has another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid hands-on practice** and accurate vacancy/pay information would help Yara decide whether maintenance is viable.
